problems.question: Is $51$ a prime number? Explain why or why not.
problems.answer: No, $51$ is not prime. $51 = 3 \times 17$, so it has factors $1, 3, 17, 51$ — more than two distinct factors.

problems.question: Find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of $24$ and $60$.
problems.answer: Prime factorisation: $$24 = 2^3 \times 3$$ $$60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5$$ Common primes with smallest powers: $2^2 \times 3 = 4 \times 3 = 12$. The HCF is $12$.

problems.question: Find the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of $18$ and $24$.
problems.answer: Prime factorisation: $$18 = 2 \times 3^2$$ $$24 = 2^3 \times 3$$ Each prime to the largest power: $2^3 \times 3^2 = 8 \times 9 = 72$. The LCM is $72$.

problems.question: Two buses leave a station at the same time. One bus completes a route every $36$ minutes and the other every $48$ minutes. After how many minutes will they next leave together?
problems.answer: We need the LCM of $36$ and $48$. $$36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$$ $$48 = 2^4 \times 3$$ LCM $= 2^4 \times 3^2 = 16 \times 9 = 144$. They will next depart together after $144$ minutes (or $2$ hours $24$ minutes).

problems.question: Find the smallest positive integer $n$ such that $126 \times n$ is a perfect square.
problems.answer: Prime factorise $126$: $$126 = 2 \times 63 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7 = 2^1 \times 3^2 \times 7^1$$ For a perfect square, all exponents must be even. Currently: $2^1$ (odd), $3^2$ (even), $7^1$ (odd). We need to multiply by $2^1 \times 7^1 = 14$. So $n = 14$. Check: $126 \times 14 = 1764 = 42^2$. ✓

problems.question: Prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers. (Hint: assume there are finitely many primes $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$ and consider $p_1 \times p_2 \times \dots \times p_n + 1$.)
problems.answer: Assume the set of primes is finite: $\{p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n\}$. Consider $N = p_1 \times p_2 \times \dots \times p_n + 1$. $N$ is greater than any of the primes. When we divide $N$ by any $p_i$, it leaves a remainder of $1$. So $N$ is not divisible by any known prime. Therefore either $N$ itself is prime (contradiction — it's not in our list) or $N$ has a prime factor not in our list (contradiction — our list was supposedly complete). Either way, our assumption was false; there must be infinitely many primes.

problems.question: Find all positive integers $n$ such that $n^2 - 1$ is prime.
problems.answer: $n^2 - 1 = (n-1)(n+1)$. For this to be prime, one factor must be $1$ (since primes have exactly two factors: $1$ and themselves). Case 1: $n-1 = 1 \Rightarrow n = 2$. Then $n^2 - 1 = 3$, which is prime. Case 2: $n+1 = 1 \Rightarrow n = 0$, but $n$ must be positive. So the only solution is $n = 2$.
